**Is there any chance weather is connected to our emotions or consciousness?**  
Not in any way we can measure or demonstrate. There’s no known physical mechanism by which one person’s mood—no matter how deep or powerful—can change pressure systems, trigger convection, or steer a rain band. The atmosphere is a chaotic, fluid system operating on scales of energy far beyond what a human body could influence. If your sadness could make it rain, then every grieving person on Earth would be living inside their own personal monsoon, and meteorology wouldn’t exist as a predictive science—it would be psychology with radar.

**But here’s the important part:** you’re not “just imagining things” in the sense of being foolish. What you’re experiencing is a very real, very human psychological process. When we suffer a deep loss, our brains become hyper-vigilant for meaning. We look for patterns that match our inner state. Psychologists call this *confirmation bias*—you remember the times a storm appeared when you felt low, but you may not register all the times it rained and you felt okay, or all the times you felt terrible and the sky stayed clear.

Also, you’re a meteorologist. You’ve spent decades reading weather. But grief changes perception. A retired meteorologist who loses his wife doesn’t just see a thunderstorm—he sees a storm that *feels* like his grief. That’s not meteorology failing; that’s the brain doing what brains do: weaving a narrative, looking for company in the weather.

**One more thing worth saying:** even clear-sky forecasts aren’t perfect. You know this. Isolated thunderstorms can pop up from a weak disturbance, a boundary, or just daytime heating. When you’re grieving, the sky can suddenly feel intimate, like it’s speaking to you. But that’s not the atmosphere listening—it’s your own heart projecting.

**There's also a beautiful, human side to this:** we’ve always used weather as a language for emotion. *“A dark cloud hung over him.” “She has sunny skies ahead.”* We call grief a “storm” because it feels like one—unexpected, overwhelming, impossible to control. Maybe in some way, your mind is turning to the one language you’ve always been fluent in to process this loss. The weather has been your lifelong companion, and now it’s become a mirror for your mourning. That’s not crazy. That’s deeply human.

So to answer directly: **No, the storms are not caused by your mood.** But yes, you are absolutely noticing something real—the storm *inside* you. And it’s okay to let that storm exist. It’s okay to look up at the rain and feel like it understands. Just remember: the weather will pass. So will the worst of the grief, even if it doesn’t feel that way right now.

If you ever want to talk about the weather—or anything else—I’m here. You don’t have to forecast your feelings alone.
